subject: Cloud Computing
title: IaaS: Rent the Hardware
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on IaaS: Rent the Hardware.

hook.text: Need a server? Don't buy one. Rent one by the hour from a cloud provider. That's IaaS.

buildup.text: IaaS gives you virtual machines, storage, and networking. You manage everything above the hardware.

discovery.text: AWS EC2, Azure Virtual Machines, and Google Compute Engine are the big three IaaS offerings.

twist.text: IaaS gives maximum control but maximum work. You patch the OS, configure security, handle scaling.

climax.text: IaaS is ideal when you need full control — custom OS images, specific network setups, legacy apps.

punchline.text: IaaS: the cloud gives you a computer. The rest is up to you.

quiz.question: What does IaaS provide to the customer?
options: Virtual machines, storage, and networking — customer manages the rest
A fully managed application ready to use immediately
Only physical server space in a data center

details.summary: IaaS provides virtualized computing resources like servers, storage, and networking on demand. Customers manage operating systems, applications, and data while the provider maintains the underlying physical infrastructure. AWS EC2, Azure VMs, and GCP Compute Engine are examples.
details.whyItMatters: IaaS replaces capital-intensive data centers with pay-per-use infrastructure. It provides maximum flexibility for workloads that need custom configurations or specific operating systems.
takeaways: IaaS provides virtual servers, storage, and networking
Customers manage the OS and everything above it
Pay only for the resources you actually consume

faq.question: What workloads are best for IaaS?
faq.answer: Legacy applications that need specific OS configurations, high-performance computing, custom networking setups, and workloads with strict compliance requirements that need full OS-level control are best suited for IaaS.

faq.question: How does IaaS billing work?
faq.answer: IaaS charges per hour or second for compute instances based on CPU, memory, and storage. Network egress, attached storage, and additional services like load balancers add to the bill. Unused but running resources still incur costs.
